description: Segregation in law, lynchings in practice and the Klan's 1920s revival — racial backlash exposed.
content_html:
Jim Crow America

Throughout the 1920s, the majority of African Americans lived under a system of legal and social oppression enforced across the South and, in different forms, throughout much of the country. The Jim Crow laws mandated separation of the races in schools, transport, restaurants, hospitals, and public spaces. The Supreme Court’s 1896 ruling in Plessy v Ferguson had declared “separate but equal” facilities constitutional — in practice, Black facilities were always inferior and the equality was fiction.

Key Fact

Jim Crow laws in the South denied African Americans equal access to education, barred them from voting through literacy tests, poll taxes, and grandfather clauses, prohibited interracial marriage, and enforced segregation in virtually all public spaces. Employment discrimination kept most Black workers in the lowest-paid, most insecure jobs regardless of their qualifications. The economic consequences were reinforced by physical terror: according to records maintained by the Tuskegee Institute, 3,446 Black Americans were lynched between 1882 and 1968, with the highest rates in the period before and after the First World War.

The Klan’s Second Revival

The original Ku Klux Klan had been suppressed in the 1870s. In 1915, a new organisation calling itself the Ku Klux Klan was refounded at Stone Mountain, Georgia, partly inspired by D.W. Griffith’s film The Birth of a Nation (1915), which portrayed the original Klan as heroic. This second Klan was broader in scope than its predecessor: it targeted not only African Americans but also Catholics, Jews, immigrants, and anyone it characterised as morally degenerate.

The Klan grew explosively in the early 1920s. By 1924 to 1925, membership had reached an estimated 4 to 6 million, with significant strength outside the South — in Indiana, Ohio, and Oregon as well as the traditional strongholds of the former Confederacy. Indiana Grand Dragon D.C. Stephenson built a powerful political machine that influenced state government and claimed to have elected congressmen and a governor.

The most devastating single act of racial violence in the 1920s occurred in Tulsa, Oklahoma, in May–June 1921. Greenwood, a prosperous African American neighbourhood known as “Black Wall Street,” was attacked by a white mob that included some deputised civilians. Homes and businesses were burned, and aircraft may have been used to fire on the neighbourhood. The 2001 Oklahoma Commission, established to investigate the events, concluded that at least 36 people died (other estimates are substantially higher) and roughly 35 blocks of Greenwood were destroyed. The event had been largely suppressed from public memory for decades. Tulsa city government officially adopted the term “massacre” in 2001 — use this framing rather than the older term “riot,” which implies mutual combat rather than an organised attack on a community.

Red Summer 1919 and the Context of Violence

The racial violence of the 1920s did not emerge from nowhere. The summer of 1919 — known as the Red Summer — saw race riots in at least 25 American cities, including Chicago and Washington DC. African American soldiers who had served in France came home expecting greater respect and rights; they encountered instead intensified racial hostility. The NAACP, led by James Weldon Johnson and W.E.B. Du Bois, documented and publicised these outrages, campaigning for a federal anti-lynching law. Every such bill was filibustered to death in the Senate by Southern politicians through the entire period covered by this unit.

Key Fact

The Klan’s membership collapsed after 1925 for several reasons. D.C. Stephenson, the Indiana Grand Dragon, was convicted of rape and second-degree murder in 1925 after the death of a woman he had assaulted on a train. His conviction destroyed the Klan’s claim to stand for moral decency. Press exposure of corruption among Klan-affiliated politicians, and internal factional fighting, accelerated the decline. By the late 1920s, membership had fallen from millions to a few hundred thousand.

African Americans responded to racial violence and oppression in multiple ways. The NAACP, led by W.E.B. Du Bois (who edited its magazine The Crisis) and James Weldon Johnson, pursued legal and political strategies. Marcus Garvey’s Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) offered a different vision: Black economic self-sufficiency and ultimately a return to Africa, encapsulated in his “Back to Africa” movement. At its peak in the early 1920s, the UNIA had claimed several million members worldwide, though these figures were disputed. The Great Migration, in which around 1.6 million African Americans moved from the South to northern cities between 1910 and 1930, was itself a form of resistance — leaving the most oppressive conditions — though discrimination followed them North.
exam_tip_html: Questions on racial violence and the Klan require you to apply impartiality: present the Klan’s revival as a historical reality without either sensationalising or minimising it. Frame the Klan as a product of specific historical conditions — post-war anxiety, nativism, and the threat white supremacists perceived from African American migration and assertion. Always use “Tulsa Race Massacre” (not “riot”). When answering questions about African American responses, distinguish between the NAACP’s legal/political approach, Garvey’s nationalist separatism, and the Great Migration as an economic response — examiners reward students who show multiple strategies.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Jim Crow laws imposed legal segregation across the South, with lynching as physical terror: the Tuskegee Institute records 3,446 Black Americans lynched between 1882 and 1968.
  • The second Ku Klux Klan, refounded in 1915, reached 4–6 million members by the mid-1920s, extending far beyond the South and targeting Catholics, Jews, and immigrants as well as African Americans, before collapsing after the Stephenson scandal of 1925.
  • African Americans responded through the NAACP’s legal strategies, Garvey’s UNIA movement, and the Great Migration, but anti-lynching bills were repeatedly filibustered and formal equality remained entirely out of reach.

practice_questions.text: Outline two features of the Jim Crow system of laws in 1920s America.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Each feature scores 1 mark for identification and 1 additional mark for specific supporting detail. Example features: legal segregation in public spaces and education (1), justified by the 1896 Plessy v Ferguson ruling that ‘separate but equal’ was constitutional, although in practice Black facilities were always inferior (1); denial of the vote through literacy tests, poll taxes, and grandfather clauses (1), meaning that African Americans in the South were effectively excluded from political participation despite the 15th Amendment (1). Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Ku Klux Klan grew so rapidly in the early 1920s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both reasons fully explained with specific evidence (e.g. post-war anxiety and the Red Summer of 1919 created a climate of racial and social fear in which the Klan’s message of ‘100 per cent Americanism’ appealed to white Protestants threatened by immigration and African American assertion; the Klan’s broadened appeal — targeting Catholics, Jews, and immigrants as well as Black Americans — allowed it to recruit millions outside the South, reaching 4–6 million by 1924–25). Secure: Both reasons explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One explained well, one identified only. Emerging: One or both identified without causal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Tulsa Race Massacre of 1921 is significant for understanding racial violence in 1920s America.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains the significance of the Tulsa Massacre in showing the scale of organised racial violence (at least 36 dead, 35 blocks destroyed); the active role of deputised civilians and the failure of authorities to protect Black residents; the deliberate suppression of the event from public memory for decades; and what this reveals about the systematic nature of racial violence rather than isolated incidents. Secure: Two or more dimensions explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One dimension explained, others listed. Emerging: General statement about the massacre’s seriousness without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA).
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature identified, plus 1 mark per supporting detail. Feature 1: The UNIA promoted Black economic self-sufficiency (1); Garvey established Black-owned businesses including a steamship company as part of his vision for Black economic independence (1). Feature 2: The UNIA promoted a ‘Back to Africa’ movement (1); Garvey argued that African Americans could never achieve equality in a white-dominated America and should instead build a new nation in Africa (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the 1920s was a decade of racial backlash in the United States? Use your knowledge and any interpretations you have studied to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that acknowledges evidence of backlash (Klan revival, Tulsa Massacre, Red Summer, Jim Crow, failed anti-lynching legislation) while also recognising African American resistance and cultural achievement (NAACP campaigns, Garvey movement, Harlem Renaissance, Great Migration); uses specific evidence throughout and engages with at least one interpretation. Secure: Clear argument addressing both backlash and resistance with relevant evidence. Developing: Some awareness of both with basic evidence; may be one-sided. Emerging: Descriptive account without structured argument. SPaG: 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Compare the following two interpretations of the Ku Klux Klan revival. Interpretation A argues the Klan reflected deep-rooted racism in American society and government. Interpretation B argues it was primarily a product of specific post-war anxieties that disappeared once conditions changed. How far do the interpretations differ, and what might explain their differences?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies key differences (structural racism vs. contingent anxiety, permanence vs. transience of the threat); uses own knowledge to evaluate both (persistence of Jim Crow and failure of anti-lynching bills for A; Klan collapse after Stephenson scandal and specific post-war context for B); explains why interpretations differ (different focus on cause, different evidence base, period of writing). Secure: Explains differences with relevant own knowledge. Developing: Identifies some differences and supports one. Emerging: Summarises each without explaining differences.

glossary_terms.definition: A system of laws and social customs in the American South that enforced racial segregation and denied Black citizens equal access to education, employment, housing, and the vote.

A white supremacist organisation refounded in 1915 at Stone Mountain, Georgia, which reached a peak membership of approximately 4 to 6 million by the mid-1920s, targeting not only Black Americans but also Catholics, Jews, and immigrants.
The Indiana state leader of the Klan who was convicted of rape and murder in 1925 — his conviction triggered the Klan's rapid collapse as it exposed the organisation's moral hypocrisy.
The summer of 1919 when at least 25 race riots erupted across the USA, as returning Black veterans who had fought in the First World War encountered white hostility and racial violence.
The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, founded in 1909, which used legal challenges and political lobbying to fight racial segregation and violence.
